translation.noHistory: Complete a hand to begin your review.
translation.welcome: Play a hand. Understand one decision.
translation.welcomeBody: Start a hand, use Check or Call when available, then open the calculation. Your goal is clear reasoning, not recovering chips.
translation.potOddsHelp: P is the pot before your call, including the current opposing bet. C is your additional call. Break-even equity = C / (P + C). Past contributions are already in P.
translation.equityHelp: Equity is your expected share of the pot, including ties. It depends on the cards and ranges entered, not a prediction of the next result.
translation.outsHelp: An out is a target card for a stated draw. Hitting it does not automatically mean winning; an opponent may improve too.
translation.storageHelp: Progress stays in this browser profile and origin. localhost and 127.0.0.1 have separate storage. Export a backup before changing browser or clearing data.
translation.heuristicHelp: Local opponents use strategy heuristics. They are not GTO solvers. Showdown equity alone cannot select every multistreet action.
translation.resetWarning: Export a backup first. Reset permanently removes this browser’s HIL progress and saved hands.

translation.lessons.HIL-001.title: Five cards decide
translation.lessons.HIL-001.prompt: In Hold’em, how many cards form your final ranked hand?
translation.lessons.HIL-001.explanation: Exactly five. Choose the strongest five from your two hole cards and five board cards; you may use zero, one or two hole cards. Seven cards are available, but seven are not ranked as a hand.
translation.lessons.HIL-002.title: The low ace
translation.lessons.HIL-002.prompt: A♣ 2♦ 3♥ 4♠ 5♣ is a straight. What is its highest rank? Enter 2–14; ace = 14.
translation.lessons.HIL-002.explanation: This is a five-high straight, called a wheel. The ace acts below the deuce here. It does not make an ace-high straight; Q-K-A-2-3 is not a straight.
translation.lessons.HIL-003.title: One pair, next card
translation.lessons.HIL-003.prompt: Board: K♣ K♦ 7♥ 4♠ 2♣. Seat 1: A♥ Q♥. Seat 2: A♠ J♠. Which seat wins?
translation.lessons.HIL-003.explanation: Both have K-K-A. The next kicker is Q versus J, so seat 1 wins with K-K-A-Q-7. The shared ace does not make the hands equal.
translation.lessons.HIL-004.title: The board belongs to everyone
translation.lessons.HIL-004.prompt: The board is A♠ K♠ Q♠ J♠ T♠. Three players reach showdown. What percentage of the pot is each player entitled to before integer odd-chip allocation?
translation.lessons.HIL-004.explanation: All play the same royal flush on the board: each has 1/3 = 33.333…% equity. Hole-card rank and suit cannot break this tie. Integer odd chips follow the published table rule.
translation.lessons.HIL-005.title: Count the suit
translation.lessons.HIL-005.prompt: You see four hearts among your two cards and the flop. No other cards are known. How many hearts remain as flush target cards?
translation.lessons.HIL-005.explanation: There are 13 hearts in a deck, so 13 − 4 = 9 target cards. These are target outs, not guaranteed winning outs: a paired board or a stronger flush can matter.
translation.lessons.HIL-006.title: One card from the flop
translation.lessons.HIL-006.prompt: There are 47 unknown cards and 9 fixed target outs. What is the probability of hitting a target on the next card? Enter a percentage.
translation.lessons.HIL-006.explanation: 9/47 × 100 = 19.1489…%. The denominator is the unknown-card count at this decision. This is a target-hit probability, not automatically the probability of winning.
translation.lessons.HIL-007.title: Two chances without replacement
translation.lessons.HIL-007.prompt: With 47 unknown cards and 9 fixed targets, you will see two cards without further decisions. What is the chance of at least one target, in percent?
translation.lessons.HIL-007.explanation: Subtract missing twice from 1: 1 − C(38,2)/C(47,2) = 378/1081 = 34.9676…%. Adding 9/47 twice double-counts some outcomes and ignores removal. Fixed targets and two cards seen are required.
translation.lessons.HIL-008.title: The turn changes the denominator
translation.lessons.HIL-008.prompt: On the turn, 46 cards are unknown and 9 target outs are still available. What is the river target-hit percentage?
translation.lessons.HIL-008.explanation: 9/46 × 100 = 19.5652…%. Use the current information set. Reusing 47 after seeing the turn would include a card that is now known.
translation.lessons.HIL-009.title: A mental shortcut has a label
translation.lessons.HIL-009.prompt: Using the approximate rule of four, what percentage do 9 flop outs suggest for seeing two cards?
translation.lessons.HIL-009.explanation: 9 × 4 = 36%, an APPROXIMATION. The fixed-target exact value is about 34.97%. The shortcut is not an equity solver and assumes two cards will be seen.
translation.lessons.HIL-010.title: All starting hands
translation.lessons.HIL-010.prompt: How many unordered two-card combinations can be drawn from 52 distinct cards?
translation.lessons.HIL-010.explanation: C(52,2) = 52 × 51 / 2 = 1326. Divide by two because A♠K♣ and K♣A♠ are the same hand. The 169 grid cells are hand classes, not concrete combinations.
translation.lessons.HIL-011.title: Pocket pairs
translation.lessons.HIL-011.prompt: Before any blockers, how many concrete combinations belong to QQ?
translation.lessons.HIL-011.explanation: Choose two of four queens: C(4,2) = 6. Four is the number of queens, not the number of pairs.
translation.lessons.HIL-012.title: Suited combinations
translation.lessons.HIL-012.prompt: Before blockers, how many concrete combinations belong to AKs, where s means suited?
translation.lessons.HIL-012.explanation: One suited ace-king per suit gives 4. AKs excludes the 12 offsuit combinations; AK without a suffix includes both in HIL notation.
translation.lessons.HIL-013.title: Offsuit combinations
translation.lessons.HIL-013.prompt: Before blockers, how many combinations belong to AKo, where o means offsuit?
translation.lessons.HIL-013.explanation: Each of four aces can pair with three kings of another suit: 4 × 3 = 12. The four suited hands are excluded.
translation.lessons.HIL-014.title: Your ace removes possibilities
translation.lessons.HIL-014.prompt: You hold A♠ 7♦. No other aces are known. How many AA combinations remain for an opponent?
translation.lessons.HIL-014.explanation: Only three aces remain available: C(3,2) = 3. Remove known cards before normalizing range weights. Do not remove simulator-only hidden cards.
translation.lessons.HIL-015.title: Every fixed-hand flop runout
translation.lessons.HIL-015.prompt: Both two-card hands and three flop cards are known, with no other known dead cards. How many unordered turn/river runouts exist?
translation.lessons.HIL-015.explanation: 52 − 2 − 2 − 3 = 45 available cards. C(45,2) = 990. This unordered count works for terminal showdown equity, where turn/river order does not change the final hand; street decisions need order.
translation.lessons.HIL-016.title: The price of this call
translation.lessons.HIL-016.prompt: The pot was 60. Opponent bets 20, so the current pot P is 80 and your additional call C is 20. With one pot and no further betting, what equity percentage breaks even?
translation.lessons.HIL-016.explanation: C/(P+C) = 20/(80+20) = 20%. Your call makes the final pot 100. Using 20/80 omits your call from the prize. Past contributions are sunk and must not be charged again.
translation.lessons.HIL-017.title: Expected chips from calling
translation.lessons.HIL-017.prompt: Current pot P = 80, additional call C = 20, equity E = 25%. No rake or future betting; one eligible pot. What is EV(call) relative to folding now?
translation.lessons.HIL-017.explanation: EV = E(P+C) − C = 0.25 × 100 − 20 = +5 chips. This is an expectation over outcomes, not a promise of profit on this hand. Do not subtract earlier contributions again.
translation.lessons.HIL-018.title: Below the threshold
translation.lessons.HIL-018.prompt: Use P = 80 and C = 20 again, but equity is 15%. With no future betting, what is EV(call)?
translation.lessons.HIL-018.explanation: 0.15 × (80+20) − 20 = −5 chips relative to folding. A later lucky card would not change the correctness of this calculation at the decision.
translation.lessons.HIL-019.title: A bluff with no fallback
translation.lessons.HIL-019.prompt: Pot before your bluff P0 = 100; your bet B = 50. Assume zero equity when called and no future decisions. What fold percentage breaks even?
translation.lessons.HIL-019.explanation: Set F×100 − (1−F)×50 = 0, giving F = 50/(100+50) = 1/3. More than 33.333…% folds gives positive EV. This is a break-even model, not a claim that the opponent folds that often.
translation.lessons.HIL-020.title: Put a fold assumption to work
translation.lessons.HIL-020.prompt: P0 = 100, B = 50, assumed fold probability F = 40%, zero equity if called. What is bluff EV in chips?
translation.lessons.HIL-020.explanation: EV = 0.4×100 − 0.6×50 = 40 − 30 = +10. The fold frequency is an assumption. Showdown equity cannot substitute for that assumption.
translation.lessons.HIL-021.title: Ties are fractional wins
translation.lessons.HIL-021.prompt: In 100 equally likely outcomes you win alone 30 times, tie with one opponent 20 times, and lose 50 times. What is equity as a percentage?
translation.lessons.HIL-021.explanation: (30×1 + 20×1/2 + 50×0)/100 = 40%. Win frequency is 30%, tie frequency 20%, loss frequency 50%. Counting each tie as a full win would overstate equity.
translation.lessons.HIL-022.title: The smaller stack sets the contest
translation.lessons.HIL-022.prompt: Before posting blinds in a heads-up hand, one player has 240 chips and the other has 90. What is the effective stack?
translation.lessons.HIL-022.explanation: min(240,90) = 90 chips per player can be contested against each other. The larger stack cannot win more than the smaller opponent owns in this hand.
translation.lessons.HIL-023.title: Heads-up changes the blinds
translation.lessons.HIL-023.prompt: Heads-up: seat 1 is button/small blind; seat 2 is big blind. Both can act. Which seat acts first preflop?
translation.lessons.HIL-023.explanation: Button/small blind acts first preflop, then last after the flop. Position changes the information available when deciding, but does not itself supply an exact action strategy.
translation.lessons.HIL-024.title: A future payment is an assumption
translation.lessons.HIL-024.prompt: Toy model: P = 80, C = 20, hit probability 10%. On a hit you always win and collect an extra 100 from the opponent; on a miss you lose with no more payment. What is call EV?
translation.lessons.HIL-024.explanation: 0.10×(80+20+100) − 20 = 0. Future opponent payment is conditional on hitting and winning. Real opponents may not pay, targets may be dirty, and your future contributions must also be accounted for.
translation.lessons.HIL-025.title: A costly second-best hand
translation.lessons.HIL-025.prompt: In a toy model, a call has baseline EV +5 chips. Separately, 10% of all outcomes cost an extra 80 chips when a second-best hand pays later. What is adjusted EV?
translation.lessons.HIL-025.explanation: 5 − 0.10×80 = −3 chips. This reverse-implied-odds term is a supplied assumption, not something raw showdown equity predicts. Do not count the same future loss twice.
translation.lessons.HIL-026.title: Eligibility comes before equity
translation.lessons.HIL-026.prompt: Three players commit 30, 80 and 80 chips. The player with 30 is all-in. How many chips are in the main pot all three can win?
translation.lessons.HIL-026.explanation: 3×30 = 90 in the main pot; 2×50 = 100 in the side pot. The short stack has no claim on that side pot. A single win percentage cannot describe both eligibility sets.
translation.lessons.HIL-027.title: Weights apply to combinations
translation.lessons.HIL-027.prompt: An unblocked range has AA at weight 100% and KK at weight 50%, with all other hands excluded. What percentage of its normalized probability is AA?
translation.lessons.HIL-027.explanation: AA contributes 6×1 = 6 weight units; KK contributes 6×0.5 = 3. AA probability is 6/(6+3) = 66.666…%. A cell weight is not itself its final probability.
translation.lessons.HIL-028.title: Overlapping target sets
translation.lessons.HIL-028.prompt: A study hand has 9 flush target cards and 8 straight target cards. Exactly 2 cards belong to both sets. How many distinct targets are there?
translation.lessons.HIL-028.explanation: 9 + 8 − 2 = 15 by inclusion-exclusion. Adding 9 and 8 without subtracting the overlap counts two cards twice. Distinct targets are still not necessarily clean winning outs.
translation.glossary.0: Weakest to strongest: high card, one pair, two pair, three of a kind, straight, flush, full house, four of a kind, straight flush. A royal flush is the highest straight flush. Equal categories compare ranks and kickers; suits never break ties.
translation.glossary.1: Expected share of a contested pot, including split pots.
translation.glossary.2: A remaining target card under stated assumptions.
translation.glossary.3: Weighted collection of possible two-card hands.
translation.glossary.4: An unpaired card used to break otherwise equal hands.
translation.glossary.5: A hand that needs a future card to make a target pattern.
translation.glossary.6: The additional call compared with the pot after calling.
translation.glossary.7: The smaller stack in a heads-up contest.
translation.glossary.8: Comparing the best five-card hands after betting ends.
